2025 RISK MANAGEMENT PLAN EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


The purpose of this plan is to describe practices in place to mitigate hazards associated with the operation of the CHS McPherson Refinery Inc. (CHS MRI) located in McPherson, Kansas.  Information in this plan is available to the Local Emergency Planning Committee, outside emergency response groups, and other interested parties.

TABLE OF CONTENTS

1.  SUMMARY
2.  ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE POLICIES
3.  DESCRIPTION OF THE STATIONARY SOURCES AND REGULATED SUBSTANCES
4.  HAZARD ASSESSMENT

1.0 SUMMARY

CHS MRI is committed to comply with all applicable health and safety regulations and conduct business in a manner which protects the people doing work under our control and the general public from harm. This document outlines the November 2025 Risk Management Plan in place at CHS MRI located at 1391 Iron Horse Road in McPherson, Kansas.  This Risk Management Plan is intended to comply with the requirements of EPA's Risk Management Program (40 CFR Part 68.) 

2.0 ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE POLICIES

CHS MRI has a long-standing commitment to worker and public safety.  This commitment is demonstrated by the resources invested in accident prevention, training of personnel, and consideration of safety in the design, installation, operation, and ma

intenance of our facility.  Our policy is to implement reasonable controls to prevent foreseeable releases of regulated substances.  However, if a release does occur, our personnel are trained to respond, control, and contain the release.

3.0 DESCRIPTION OF THE STATIONARY SOURCES AND REGULATED SUBSTANCES

CHS MRI operates a variety of processes to produce petroleum products from raw crude oil.  CHS MRI is capable of processing 115,000 barrels of crude oil per day and typically processes 11,000 barrels per day of natural gasoline. CHS MRI receives and transports petroleum products via trucks and pipelines and has a storage capacity of petroleum and refined products exceeding 1.5 million barrels in above ground tanks.

Some processes at CHS MRI contain the following regulated flammable substances in amounts greater than Risk Management Program Threshold Quantities: butane, isobutane, and propane. Most processes at CHS MRI contain mixtures of these and other flammable substances in amounts exceeding the threshold quantity.  CHI MRI also uses hydrogen fluoride in one of the refinery processes and anhydrous ammonia in the unit manufacturing fertilizers.  Hydrogen sulfide presents in many material streams but only in small quantities. 
 
4.0 HAZARD ASSESSMENT RESULTS

CHS MRI has completed all hazard assessments required under the Risk Management Program rules.   Details of the Hazard Assessment are included in the data submitted to the U.S. EPAs Central Data Exchange.  Out of the 21 CHS MRI processes subject to the RMP regulations, only four have a potential to reach the property boundaries and affect public receptors even in the worst-case release scenario.  The remaining units effects are predicted to remain limited within the facility property boundaries.

5.0 PREVENTION PROGRAM STEPS

The following is a summary of the general accident prevention program in place at CHS MRI. Because the processes at CHS MRI are regulated by the EPA Risk Management Program (RMP) regu

lation and OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM) standard, this summary addresses each of the OSHA PSM elements and describes the management system in place to implement the accident prevention program.

Leadership and Commitment
At CHS, we strive for excellence in environmental, health, and safety (EHS) by living out our core values of Integrity, Safety, Cooperative Spirit, and Inclusion. The health and safety of people, communities, and environment are at the forefront of what we do every day. We believe EHS performance is an individual responsibility and a way of life both on and off the job.
For these reasons, we are committed to:
a)	Always working safely, regardless of urgency or importance of the task.
b)	Identifying, assessing, and effectively controlling EHS risks.
c)	Pursuing EHS excellence through inclusion and engagement of employees.
d)	Empowering everyone to take personal responsibility for their safety and the safety of others.
e)	Supporting environmental stewardship, sustainability, and community wellbeing.
f)	Complying with all EHS laws, regulations, and internal requirements.
g)	Implementing a management system that promotes continual improvement in EHS performance.
h)	Providing the necessary leadership and resources to achieve our EHS objectives and targets.

The CHS MRI Vision Statement and Objectives provide direction and allow Senior Managers to develop and track Key Performance Indicators (KPI) on an annual basis.
The Vision Statement and Objectives are designed as a fixed strategy to allow the Process Safety Management System to mature, and annual Management Reviews ensure the Vision Statement and Objectives remain appropriate for current process safety threats and vulnerabilities.

KPIs allows Senior Managers and the workforce to concentrate on the strategic delivery of both the process safety performance and expectations.

Senior Managers focus on directing the Management System to assure internal and external compliance requirements are met

and to drive continual improvement. They prioritize Process Safety Plans to focus on the highest-impact items in alignment with the Vision and Objectives. They provide resources and monitor progress on Process Safety Plans all the way through completion and closeout.

Through strong leadership and by positive example, Senior Managers and all leadership encourage and facilitate alignment to the Process Safety Vision, Objectives, and Expectations throughout the workforce. This is achieved by:
	Regular communication with the workforce regarding process safety expectations, KPIs, and current performance against metrics.
	Regular interaction with the workforce in their workplace to review alignment to process safety expectations and procedures.
	Face-to-face discussions with the workforce on the applicability of written procedures to ensure their safe and effective job execution.
	Coaching the workforce where process safety expectations fall short.
	Ensuring that resources are in place to deliver process safety expectations and performance, including site verification during regular tours.

Leaders are expected to hold themselves and the workforce accountable for the delivery of process safety performance and alignment to expectations. Through the Management Review Process, the leadership team verifies that they are undertaking all the activities necessary to demonstrate full commitment and accountability.

All members of the workforce are accountable for alignment to process safety expectations and performance.

Reinforcement of the workforce commitment is delivered through POL-471-0001 Safety Responsibility. This Policy clearly defines expectations to ensure the ongoing safety of the workforce and emphasizes the requirement that all must exercise the right to stop work due to substandard conditions, work practices, or hazards.

STD-42433-0012 PSM  Process Safety Information (previously POL-42433-0063)
All process safety information (PSI) shall be up-to-date, avai

lable to the workforce, and compiled prior to the start of any PHA. The requirements include:
a)	Information on the hazards of the highly hazardous chemicals in the process considering toxicity; permissible exposure limits; physical data; reactivity data; corrosivity data; thermal and chemical stability data; and hazardous effects of inadvertent mixing of different materials.
b)	Information on the technology of the process covering block flow diagram or simplified process flow diagram; process chemistry; maximum intended inventory; safe upper and lower limits for such items as temperatures, pressures, flows, or compositions; and an evaluation of the consequences of deviations, including those affecting the safety and health of the workforce.
c)	Information on the equipment in the process covering materials of construction; piping and instrument diagrams (P&IDs); electrical classification; relief system design and design basis; ventilation system design; design codes and standards employed; material and energy balances for processes built after May 26, 1992; and safety systems (e.g., interlocks, detection, or suppression systems).
d)	Documentation that equipment complies with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices.
e)	For equipment designed and constructed in accordance with codes, standards, or practices that are no longer in general use, determination must be made and documented that the equipment is designed, maintained, inspected, tested, and operated in a safe manner.
f)	A system is in place for the storage, retention, and controlling of process safety information.

STD-42433-0009 PSM  Process Hazards Analysis (previously POL-42433-0064)
A Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) is conducted on all CHS MRI facilities to identify, evaluate, and control hazards associated with operating the facility, including offsite safety and environmental consequences. The requirements include:
a)	Prior to performing the PHA, the appropriate Process Safety Informa

tion must be compiled for reference during the PHA.
b)	One or more PHA techniques must be selected and utilized as part of the process with selection appropriate to the risks identified.
c)	PHAs must be conducted by a team with a leader who is familiar with the appropriate PHA techniques. Other team members must include a member of Process Engineering and at least one person who has knowledge of the unit from operations. Representatives from Engineering, Operations, Maintenance, Environmental, and Safety should also be considered.
d)	The PHA must address such aspects of operation as the hazards of the process; previous incidents involving the process; engineering and administrative controls to mitigate the hazards; consequences of failures of these controls; and siting and human factors including qualitative evaluations of safety and health risks to employees, the public, and environmental issues. Data on previous 5-year releases must also be included in the scope of the PHA.
e)	The PHA must provide assessment for worst-case offsite event impacts to both the public and environment.
f)	The PHA and any associated studies are documented and must include the identification of recommendations. Reports must include all details of techniques utilized, assumptions made, analytical assessment completed, and full descriptions of both onsite and offsite events.
g)	All recommendations from the PHA must be evaluated by Senior Management, and action plans must be determined. All actions must be documented, tracked to closure, and verified.
h)	All reports and records resulting from PHAs, along with the status of all study recommendations, must be retained for the life of the process and be available to all employees.
i)	At least every five (5) years after the completion of the initial process hazard analysis, the process hazard analysis must be updated and revalidated by a team meeting the standards requirements to ensure that the hazard analysis is consistent with the current pr

ocess.

STD-42433-0024 PSM  Operating Procedures (previously POL-42433-0065)
Written operating procedures must be developed and implemented with clear instructions for safely conducting all plant process activities. The procedures must also include all required process safety information. Requirements include the following:
a)	Operating procedures must address phases covering initial startup; normal operations; temporary operations; emergency shutdown, including the conditions under which emergency shutdown is required, and the assignment of shutdown responsibility to qualified operators to ensure that emergency shutdown is executed in a safe and timely manner; emergency operations; normal shutdown; and startup following a turnaround, or after an emergency shutdown.
b)	Operating procedures must address the operating limits of the plans including consequences of deviation from the operating limits and the steps required to correct or avoid deviation.
c)	Operating procedures must include health and safety considerations covering properties of, and hazards presented by, the chemicals used in the process; precautions necessary to prevent exposure, including engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment; control measures to be taken if physical contact or airborne exposure occurs; quality control for raw materials and control of hazardous chemical inventory levels; any special or unique hazards; and safety systems (e.g., interlocks, detection, or suppression systems) and their functions.
d)	Operating procedures must be up-to-date.
e)	Operating procedures must be readily accessible to the workforce.
f)	The operating procedures must be reviewed as part of any planned management of change and updated accordingly.
g)	Operating procedures must be reviewed annually and certified to ensure they are current and accurate.
h)	Safe Work Practices must be developed and implemented to mitigate and control workplace hazards for both CHS MRI staff an

d contractors. At minimum, safe work practices must cover lockout/tagout; confined space entry; opening process equipment or piping; and control over entrance into a facility by maintenance, contractor, laboratory, or other support personnel.

STD-42433-0021 PSM  Employee Participation (previously POL-42433-0062)
A series of procedures and guidelines must be in place to actively engage both the workforce and members of the public on matters relating to the Process Safety Management System as governed by current regulations. Requirements include:
a)	Consultation with the workforce and their representatives on the conduct and development of process hazard analyses.
b)	Consultation and engagement with the workforce and their representatives on the development of, and updates to, the PSMS.
c)	Workforce and their representatives provided access to PHAs and information associated with the PSMS.

STD-42433-0028 PSM  Training (previously POL-42433-0066)
Employee training and the provision of training requirements ensure that the workforce has the knowledge and skills needed to execute their job function safely. Training requirements include the following:
a)	Initial training is provided for new employees and/or existing employees operating a new process and/or equipment. The training must cover the specific safety and health hazards of the process, emergency operations including shutdown, and other safe work practices that apply to the employees job tasks.
b)	Refresher training must be provided and completed every three years at a minimum.
c)	Evaluation of the candidates understanding and knowledge retention of provided training must be completed.
d)	A record must be kept containing the identity of the employee, the date of training, and how the employer verified that the employee understood the training.
e)	Each contractor employee must also be provided with the required training with verification of knowledge retention.

STD-42433-0019 PSM  Contractors (previously PO

L-42433-0067)
A comprehensive program for the management of contractors engaged in performing maintenance or repair, turnaround, major renovation, or specialty work is required. Requirements include the following:
a)	Evaluation of the contractors performance and ability to safely execute work at CHS MRIs facility is conducted prior to engagement.
b)	Ongoing evaluation and audit of the contractors performance when working for CHS MRI is conducted periodically.
c)	Contractors must be informed of the known potential fire, explosion, or toxic release hazards related to the contractors work and the process.
d)	Contractors must be informed of the applicable provisions of the emergency action plan.
e)	Safe work practices are developed and implemented to control the presence, entrance, and exit of contractors.
f)	A contract employee injury and illness log is maintained related to the contractors work onsite.
g)	The contractor must provide documented assurance that contract employees are instructed in the known potential fire, explosion, or toxic release hazards related to their job and the process, and in the applicable provisions of the emergency action plan.
h)	The contractor must provide assurance that each contract employee follows the safety rules of the facility including the safe work practices required in the operating procedures.
i)	Contractors must inform CHS MRI of any unique hazards presented by the contract employers work.

STD-42433-0010 PSM  Pre-Startup Safety Review (previously POL-42433-0068)
A Pre-Startup Safety Review must be performed for new facilities and for modified facilities when the modification is significant enough to require a change in the process safety information. The requirements include:
a)	The assessment must take place before the introduction of hazardous chemicals and start-up of facilities in scope.
b)	Assurance the construction and equipment are in accordance with design specifications.
c)	Assurance that safety, operating, mai

ntenance, and emergency procedures are in place and are adequate.
d)	Confirmation that a hazard review has been performed, and recommendations have been resolved or implemented before startup, and modified facilities meet the management of change requirements.
e)	Assurance that training of each employee involved in operating a process has been completed.

STD-42433-0014 PSM  Mechanical Integrity (previously POL-42433-0069)
It is essential to maintain the mechanical integrity of critical process equipment to ensure it is designed and installed correctly and operates properly. Requirements include the following:
a)	Process equipment such as pressure vessels and storage tanks, piping systems (including piping components such as valves), relief and vent systems and devices, emergency shutdown systems, controls (including monitoring devices and sensors, alarms, and interlocks), and pumps are all included within scope.
b)	Written procedures must be developed and implemented to maintain the ongoing integrity of process equipment.
c)	All members of the workforce involved in maintaining the ongoing integrity of process equipment must be trained in an overview of that process and its hazards and trained in the procedures applicable to the specific job tasks.
d)	Inspection and testing must be performed on process equipment, using procedures that follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices.
e)	The frequency of inspections and tests of process equipment must conform with manufacturers recommendations and good engineering practices at minimum.
f)	A system of record must be implemented and maintained for the inspection and testing of process equipment, and must detail date of the inspection or test, the name of the person who performed the inspection or test, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment on which the inspection or test was performed, a description of the inspection or test performed, and the results of the inspection or test.
g)

Equipment deficiencies outside the acceptable limits defined by the process safety information must be corrected, or acceptable mitigation plans must be in place prior to further use.
h)	Regarding newly constructed equipment, as it is fabricated equipment, it is ensured to be suitable for the process application for which it will be used.
i)	Appropriate checks and inspections are performed to ensure that equipment is installed properly and is consistent with design specifications and the manufacturers instructions.
j)	Maintenance materials, spare parts, and equipment are ensured to be suitable for the process application for which they will be used.

STD-42433-0022 PSM  Hot Work (previously POL-42433-0070)
A Hot Work Permit must be issued for hot work operations. Requirements include the following:
a)	The permit must document that the fire prevention and protection requirements in OSHA regulations (1910.252[a]) have been fully implemented.
b)	The permit must be in place with the appropriate work authorization given prior to the start of hot work. The permit must include the date(s) authorized for hot work and must identify the object on which hot work is to be performed.
c)	The permit must be kept on file for 3 years following completion of the hot work.
 
STD-42433-0008 PSM  Management of Change (previously POL-42433-0071)
A change to a process must be thoroughly evaluated to fully assess the impact on employee safety and health, and to determine the needed changes to operating procedures. Requirements for the Management of Change include the following:
a)	A written procedure must be established and implemented to manage changes (except for replacements in kind) to process chemicals, technology, equipment, procedures, and change to facilities.
b)	Prior to any change, consideration must be given to the technical basis for the proposed change; the impact of the change on employee safety and health; modifications to operating procedures; necessary time for the ch

ange; and authorization requirements for the proposed change.
c)	Members of the workforce who operate and maintain the facility subject to change are identified and are informed of, and trained in, the change prior to startup of the process.
d)	Process safety information impacted by the change is identified and appropriately updated.
e)	Operating procedures or practices impacted by the change are identified and appropriately updated.

STD-42433-0023 PSM  Incident Investigation (previously POL-42433-0072)
A process will be implemented and maintained to report and investigate incidents that resulted in, or could reasonably have resulted in, a catastrophic release of a highly hazardous chemical. Requirements include the following:
a)	The means must be established for members of the workforce to report all such incidents immediately.
b)	Guidelines and definitions to classify the incidents must be provided.
c)	The incident investigation must commence as soon as possible, but not later than 48 hours following the incident.
d)	An Investigation Team Leader is appointed who will, in turn, appoint team members who are familiar with the facility and process, including contractors, where appropriate.
e)	Appropriate technique(s) is selected and implemented to identify the incident root causes.
f)	A report is developed for all incident investigations which at minimum will include date of incident; date investigation began; description of the incident; factors that contributed to the incident; and recommendations resulting from the investigation.
g)	The report is reviewed by all affected workforce whose job tasks are relevant to the incident findings.
h)	A system of records is implemented and maintained for all incident reports and investigations.
i)	Recommendations resulting from completed investigations are identified, documented, and tracked to closure.
j)	The incident investigation reports must be retained for 5 years.

STD-42433-0020 PSM  Emergency Planning & Response (prev

iously POL-42433-0073)
Plans and resources are in place to respond immediately and effectively to all emergency situations impacting the Refinery and surrounding area. The requirements include requirements in accordance with provisions of 29 CFR 1910.38 including the following:
a)	A written plan must be developed and implemented to cover the mitigation and control of hazards impacting site personnel and the public.
b)	At minimum, plans must be in writing and cover procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency; procedures for emergency evacuation, including type of evacuation and exit route assignments; procedures to be followed by employees who remain to operate critical plant operations before they evacuate; procedures to be followed by employees performing rescue or medical duties; and the name or job title of every employee who may be contacted by employees who need more information about the plan or an explanation of their duties under the plan.
c)	Planning must include coordination with the community emergency response plan developed under 42 U.S.C. 11003.
d)	An alarm system in line with current regulatory requirements is implemented and maintained.
e)	Training must be provided for members of the workforce with dedicated emergency response duties including assisting the evacuation of other members of the workforce.
f)	Actions required by the workforce in the event of an emergency are thoroughly communicated.
g)	Emergency response plans are tested on a periodic basis.
h)	A review of the plans is conducted for newly assigned members with emergency response duties and when the plans have changed.
i)	Procedures for handling small releases of hazardous chemicals must be established.
j)	Emergency health care, employee training measures, and procedures for informing the public and response agencies for emergency situations must be in place.
k)	Procedure to account for all employees during and following an evacuation.
 
STD-42433-0018 PSM  Compliance Audits (prev

iously POL-42433-0074)
To ensure the ongoing effectiveness of the management system and compliance with both regulations and internal requirements, a comprehensive compliance audit program will be in place. The requirements include:
a)	An audit plan must be developed to ensure the entire system is audited at least every three (3) years.
b)	Compliance audits must be conducted by individuals who have been trained and are knowledgeable in the process.
c)	The completed compliance audits must be formally documented in a report and must include details on any identified gaps/non-compliances.
d)	Gaps/non-compliances revealed during an audit must identify and list specific corrective actions.  Accepted corrective actions must be tracked to closure.
e)	The two most recent compliance audit reports must be kept on file.

STD-42433-0027 PSM  Trade Secrets (previously POL-42433-0075)
Relevant information including Trade Secrets/Proprietary Information will be made available to workforce members responsible for compiling the process safety information, those developing the process hazard analysis, those responsible for developing the operating procedures, and those performing incident investigations, emergency planning and response, and compliance audits. The requirements include:
a)	Verification is required to confirm that all requests to access information deemed as Trade Secrets/Proprietary Information are for the intended use of this requirement.
b)	All personnel accessing Trade Secrets/Proprietary Information must sign a Confidentiality Agreement.

6.0 CHEMICAL RISK MANAGEMENT STEPS

The processes at CHS MRI have hazards that are managed to assure continued safe operation.  The accident prevention program summarized previously is applied to all Program 3 EPA RMP-covered processes at CHS MRI.  Collectively, these prevention program activities help prevent potential accident scenarios that could be caused by natural forces, equipment failures, and/or human errors.

In additio

n to the accident prevention program activities, CHS MRI has safety features on many units to quickly detect a release, contain/control a release, and reduce the consequences of (mitigate) a release.  The following types of safety features are used in various processes:

Release Detection
1.  Hydrocarbon (crude oil products) detectors with alarms
2.  Hydrogen Fluoride and Hydrogen Sulfide detectors with alarms
3.  Process instrumentation with alarms
4.  Twenty-four hour/day monitoring or processes by process unit operators.

Release Containment/Control
1.  Process relief valves that discharge to a flare where releases are combusted
2.  Valves to permit isolation of the process (manual and/or automated)
3.  Automated shutdown systems for specific process parameters (e.g., high level, high temperature)
4.  Vessels to permit partial removal of the process inventory in the event of a release
5.  Curbing or diking to contain liquid releases
6.  Redundant equipment and instrumentation (e.g., uninterruptible power supply for process control system, backup firewater pump)
7.  Atmospheric relief devices

Release and Fire Mitigation
1.  Refinery fire water system
      -Diesel driven fire water pumps
      -Electric driven fire water pumps
      -Fire hydrants with permanently mounted water monitors throughout Refinery
      -Firefighting foam stations
2.  Fixed deluge systems for specific process equipment
3.  Trained emergency response teams (24-hour on call)
      -Emergency Response Team 
      -Rescue Team
      -Hazardous Materials Team
      -Emergency Medical Team
4.  Emergency Response Equipment
      -6000 gpm firefighting pumper truck
      -3500 gpm firefighting pumper truck
      -6000 gpm aerial firefighting pumper trucks
      -Ambulance  or medic unit
      -2000 gpm quick attack 1
      -Dual 2000 gpm quick attack 2 equipped with 4  foam totes
      -Dual 2000 gpm hazmat/quick attack
      -Rescue/brush truck
      -Foam tender equipped with 6  foam totes

-Hose tender
      -5500 gpm sub/boost pump
      -3000 gpm submersible pump sub trailer
      -6x9 trailer tsunami deck gun trailer mounted
      -1500 lbs PurpleK dry chem trailer
      -6000 psi Bauer air compressor 
      -1600 gal foam trailers
      -Hazardous materials response trailer
      
5.  Personal protective equipment for personnel

HF Alkylation Unit Active Mitigation Equipment
1.  Closed circuit unit television system monitored 24 hours/day by operators
2.  Remote operated valves for containment of hydrogen fluoride in event of leak
3.  Elevated deluge monitors around hydrogen fluoride area
4.  Deluge system on hydrogen fluoride pumps and gauge glasses
5.  Fire hydrant mounted monitors around hydrogen fluoride storage
6.  Administrative control to minimize amount of hydrogen fluoride in storage

Other Items to Prevent or Mitigate a Release/Fire
1.  Mutual aid agreements with local emergency agencies
2.  Routine training for Emergency Response Teams
      -Classroom training
      -Field training
3.  Employees are trained on emergency response duties through:
      -Classroom training
      -Field training
      -Computer-based training
4.  Refinery emergency notification systems
      -Refinery emergency outdoor warning system
      -Pager system for process units and emergency personnel
      -Multi-channel employee handheld radio system
      -Refinery emergency telephone number answered by 24-hour dispatch
5.  Preventive maintenance program for Refinery process equipment
6.  Scheduled maintenance and testing of emergency equipment and systems
7.  Onsite Refinery engineering staff to assure equipment and processes comply with latest specifications
8.  Scheduled Refinery shutdown for maintenance (4 to 5 year schedule)
9.  Full time Environment, Health and Safety staff

7.0 FIVE YEAR ACCIDENT HISTORY

During the last five years, no accidents have occurred involving a reportable release of regulated substances.  

8.0 EMERGENCY RESPONSE PROGRAM

INFORMATION

CHS MRI maintains a written Emergency Response Plan to ensure a coordinated and timely response to chemical releases, fires, explosions, natural disasters as well as other emergencies.  This type of response is necessary to protect public and workers safety, as well as the environment.  Items covered in the plan include emergency notification and response of employees, notification of local emergency response agencies and the public, first-aid and emergency medical care, evacuation plans and routes, accounting of personnel after an evacuation, emergency equipment list, inspection, testing and maintenance of emergency equipment, and employee emergency plan training requirements.  The emergency response program is reviewed annually and updated as needed.  The overall emergency response program for CHS MRI is coordinated with the McPherson County Local Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC).  This committee is comprised of local emergency response officials, industry representatives and other concerned citizens.  CHS MRI has a representative on this committee.

CHS MRI has the capability to communicate with McPherson County Emergency Management officials and emergency response organizations by telephone and handheld radios.  This provides a means of notifying the public of an incident, if necessary, as well as facilitating quick response to an incident.  In addition to participating in LEPC meetings, CHS MRI conducts periodic emergency drills that involve the LEPC and emergency response organizations and holds annual or semi-annual coordination meetings.  The Refinery provides refresher training to local emergency responders regarding the hazards of regulated substances in the Refinery.

9.0 PLANNED CHANGES TO IMPROVE SAFETY

CHS MRI is constantly looking for ways to improve safety and decrease possible exposure to chemicals.   Regular audits, safety information reviews and process hazard analyses provide the facility with a systematic approach to identify ch

anges to improve safety, and to track and document the implementation of such changes.   

CHS MRI continues to work on development of a Safety Culture Change program.   A Union/Management Guidance team provides the leadership for this program.  Multiple Grass Roots employee-directed teams have been organized and are working on safety projects throughout the facility.

CHS MRI continues to improve four key areas: infrastructure, response equipment, training, and document control. 

CHS MRI routinely reviews fire water demands. As a result, CHS MRI continuously strives to improve underground piping, hydrant manifold configurations, and fire water supply. CHS MRI recently completed the installation of a new fire water tank and additional fire pumps. On a parallel path, CHS MRI invested in a 3000-gpm submersible pump to augment fire water supply. The submersible pump enables CHS MRI to use static water sources, if necessary. CHS MRI routinely reviews deluge systems throughout the facility and upgrades are planned and completed as needed.  

CHS MRI routinely reviews response equipment. As a result, CHS MRI continuously strives to improve response equipment capability. 

CHS MRI routinely reviews response training. As a result, CHS MRI continuously strives to improve ERT training. Previously, CHS MRI completed a 4-million-dollar fire training facility that allows for robust training programs to be provided to CHS MRI ERT members. Since February 2019, courses and certifications have been given in the following areas:
o	Industrial Firefighting
o	Incident Command
o	Driver/Operator
o	HAZMAT Awareness
o	HAZMAT Operations

CHS MRI continues to leverage existing and recently developed and implemented management system tools to enhance documentation of key Health, Safety, PSM, and Emergency Response activities following the traditional Plan, Do, Check, Act philosophy.

CHS MRI continuously reviews and revises a 5-year plan focusing on fire apparatus and equipment enhancements.
Starting 2024 and into the future, CHS MRI will conduct annual notification drills and periodic tabletop and field exercises with the local responders.
